title: The Yang Mun Shock: The Monk in Your Feed Has a Checkout Page

# The Yang Mun Shock: The Monk in Your Feed Has a Checkout Page

*One quiet 65-second video leads to a paid journey and three eBooks. Public sources still disagree about who is speaking.*

The camera barely moves. A monk sits before an open book and candles, looks straight at the viewer, and speaks as if the two of them have a minute alone. In 65 seconds, “Words of Motivation from Yang Mun” moves from worry about the future to a small morning-and-night reflection.

Public YouTube metadata captured on 21 October 2026 showed 521,549 views for the Short. That number tells us how many times it had been watched at that snapshot. It does not tell us how many people bought anything.

The next tap changes the scene. On Yang Mun’s profile, the link leads to a paid program and a bundle of books. Then another question appears: is the monk a synthetic character, or a real teacher speaking through an AI-translated voice? The public sources give different answers.

## Is the monk AI, or is the voice AI? The explanations conflict.

[HeyGen’s customer story](https://www.heygen.com/customer-stories/yangmun) describes Yang Mun as an AI character created with HeyGen by Shalev Hani. [Columbia News Service](https://columbianewsservice.com/2026/03/24/millions-found-comfort-in-a-buddhist-monk-but-he-was-never-real/) also describes a generated character and identifies Hani as its creator.

But a [first-party page linked by Columbia](https://www.yangmuns.com/blog/the-truth-behind-%E2%80%9Ctime-to-heal%E2%80%9D-by-yang-mun) says Yang Mun is a real teacher and only the voice is translated with AI. That conflicts with both the vendor case study and the reporting. The available pages do not settle the disagreement, so this article does not present either version as independently proven.

## The creator is named. The audience numbers have dates.

Hani is the creator named by HeyGen and Columbia. His [X account](https://x.com/shalevhvs) is the creator’s profile, separate from Yang Mun’s accounts. The public Instagram handle is [@yangmunus](https://www.instagram.com/yangmunus/), and the [YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@Yangmunv2) is @Yangmunv2. Columbia reported about 2.5 million Instagram followers in March 2026. On 21 October, the YouTube page showed about 159,000 subscribers and 172 videos. A supplied screenshot shows that the channel joined YouTube on 4 November 2025; that is a channel date, not proof of when Yang Mun first appeared.

The channel page and its Shorts listing do not show the same number. A flat yt-dlp listing of the [Shorts page](https://www.youtube.com/@Yangmunv2/shorts) returned 143 entries on 21 October. The channel page showed 172 videos. Those are different lists, not contradictory counts. Several reports mention Yang Mun TikTok accounts, but the exact handles were not established in the sources reviewed here.

## Sixty-five seconds, one steady frame, and a small action

The first Short barely changes its composition. The robe, book, candles, and temple-like background stay in place; the face and voice carry the story.

[youtube-short:Er2Ig4GM7z0|Words of Motivation from Yang Mun]

The emotional sequence is compact: acknowledge a familiar worry, name ordinary hopes around home and work, then offer a simple reflection to repeat in the morning and at night. The point is not the exact wording. It is the movement from recognition to relief to an action small enough to try.

A second clip uses a different door. The 78-second “1minute of Yang Mun Wisdom” opens with a sleep-related concern and moves toward a traditional-medicine explanation. Its metadata showed 1,102,388 views on the same date. That health claim has not been independently verified; views cannot make it medical advice.

[youtube-short:Qdv6S7HonSM|1minute of Yang Mun Wisdom]

A third video, “You’re Drinking Water the WRONG Way,” was 96 seconds long and showed 12,561,496 views in the 21 October metadata snapshot. We checked metadata only for that clip; its contents have not been assessed here. The three numbers describe reach at a moment in time, not sales, trust, or the accuracy of a claim.

## Open the profile and the habit becomes a product

The [30-Day Healing Journey page](https://www.yang-mun.com/pages/journey) displays a one-time price of $49.99. It describes five-to-ten-minute daily practices, weekly video teachings, a community, and Q&A. The page offers a $59.99 “Complete Collection” with three eBooks: “Time To Heal,” “Stillness,” and “Modern Soul.” It also presents two gifts with the Journey. These are seller-page descriptions, not independent evidence that the program improves health.

The [home page](https://www.yang-mun.com/) shows a separate $19.99 bundle. The Journey page displays counters for 30,000-plus books sold and 2,500-plus people who joined the Journey; the home page says 20,000-plus readers and “5 million” lives touched. Those labels and totals do not share a published definition or audit. They should stay as seller-displayed counters.

This is a direct path from free short video to the creator’s own checkout page. The visible purchase path is a first-party checkout. A viewer sees a repeatable character, taps the profile, and chooses between a low-priced bundle, a guided program, or a slightly larger bundle with books. The public pages show the offer design. They do not show which video caused a purchase or how many buyers kept the product.

The production promise is part of the story too. HeyGen’s customer case says a video takes about 20 minutes to produce and describes a move from several posts a week to daily publishing, summarized there as a sevenfold cadence increase. Those are vendor-published case-study claims, not an independently measured production log. Still, the mechanism is visible: one recognizable format makes frequent publishing easier, while the profile page carries the paid offer.

## Revenue, profit, and an offer are different numbers

The headline figures around Yang Mun use different periods and accounting terms. Columbia reports that Hani said revenue since launch exceeded $300,000 and that he turned down a $325,000 acquisition offer. [Virtual Humans](https://virtualhumans.org/article/who-is-yang-mun-the-ai-generated-wellness-guru-with-2-6m-followers) reports a separate claim of more than $300,000 in profit within 90 days and mentions a dashboard above $213,000 in gross revenue over three months.

A screenshot supplied for this research shows an X headline claiming $500,000 in six months; the capture does not show the exact post URL or date. Columbia also reports that Hani offered an AI-character service at $799 per hour. Each figure has a different source and scope. None comes with a reconciled, audited ledger in the public materials reviewed here.

Revenue is not profit. Gross revenue does not subtract refunds, payment fees, advertising, taxes, or production costs. An acquisition offer is not cash received, and a displayed price is not a count of purchases. A careful reader can see a large audience, products for sale, and several creator-reported figures. The reader cannot calculate net income from these pages.

## A robe carries trust before a word is spoken

A monk’s appearance can make a viewer expect spiritual knowledge before hearing a sentence. That can comfort someone who wants a calm moment. It can also mislead someone who believes the speaker is a real monk or assumes a health claim comes from a qualified teacher.

There is a useful point of comparison. [Thai PBS describes Phra Maha AI](https://www.thaipbsworld.com/around-thailand/thailands-first-virtual-monk-to-preach-buddhism-to-new-generation) as a real Thai monk who worked with programmers on a 2D animated character. A real monk using a digital character and a synthetic persona presented as a monk are different cases, even if both appear on a phone screen.

We are Buddhists, so that difference matters to us. Digital characters can carry teachings to people who may never enter a temple. Trust depends on explaining who made the character, how its words were prepared, and where reflection ends and health advice begins. A clear AI disclosure gives viewers a fair chance to understand what they are watching.

## Update, 23 October 2026: the creator's own record, and a sale

We read back Shalev Hani's public X posts and long-form articles from December 2023 to October 2026. In his [pinned April 2026 article](https://x.com/shalevhvs/status/2042242260784537736), he describes how Yang Mun began. He had been making AI content for brands. He noticed that most synthetic characters were silent images, and he asked what would happen "if an AI character actually talked" and delivered a useful message every day. He lays out a five-step system: a character who looks different and carries authority, scripts built on empathy and a specific solution, one unchanging voice, three posts a day on each platform, and digital products as the only revenue line.

His [April script article](https://x.com/shalevhvs/status/2044099931494068455) names three structures he says beat more than 200 others: the reframe ("If you're going to overthink… then overthink the positive"), "you're doing it wrong," and validation. The second one invites health claims, so it needs the most care.

The biggest change is ownership. On [16 July 2026 Hani posted](https://x.com/shalevhvs/status/2077788420240494866) that he had sold Yang Mun for $170,000. He listed 6 million followers, 22,000 buyers on an email list and a 5,000-person community. In [a longer piece](https://x.com/shalevhvs/status/2082119075095060964) he argues that the buyers, not the followers, were the asset: "The followers were the billboard." We could not verify the buyer or the terms. Readers should treat Yang Mun content posted after July 2026 as possibly made under a new owner.

These are first-person claims. His own posts describe the headline result as revenue in one place and as profit in another, and the figures differ ($300K, $467K and $500K). The new record makes the history clearer. It does not make the accounting audited. The full dated chronology, with sources, is now part of [*The Art of AI Monks*](https://aniccaai.com/the-art-of-ai-monks).

## Study the system, not someone else’s face or script

The reusable pattern is more interesting than any one line: choose a recognizable character; keep the visual frame steady; make each clip about one feeling or question; end with an action that fits the message; and give interested viewers a clear next step. Then measure what happens after the view: profile visits, link taps, purchases, refunds, and net revenue.

The sources do not establish which clip sold which product. They also do not establish that Yang Mun was the first AI monk or the largest in every language and platform. We can study the structure without copying Hani’s exact words, voice, face, or design.

The [AI Monk Index](https://aniccaai.com/ai-monk-database) now separates nine researched profiles from 66 unverified Instagram leads. Open it to check what is known, what is only reported, and what still needs evidence. The robe may stop the scroll; the receipts should decide what we believe.
